text: RE-SCOPED by the chief at 07:00Z after m1's measurement (post-01M164WB0HK1H5C7N7BR0GB5EG) falsified the original diagnosis. THE SUITE IS NOT THE PROBLEM. Same code, same pin, same machine: 317.8s during the chief's 05:15Z audit with the data volume at 100% and ~7 actors running sbt; 55.0s in m1's run at load ~10 with two sbt JVMs; 115.9s in m1's immediately following run at load ~13. A 2x spread between consecutive runs of identical code rules out the workload. The suite's own cost is ~55s, so making it instant would save 55s of a nine-minute audit and would NOT stop the kills - the next-longest suite would become the stall point. THE TELL, which the chief observed and misread: the sbt JVM sat at 0.0% CPU for 4.5 minutes. That is waiting, not slow computation - a contention signature, not a workload signature. ACTUAL CAUSE: multiple actors running full three-platform courts concurrently on one machine, sometimes with the disk near full, substantially because the chief was requiring full compileAll+testAll evidence per candidate. NEW SCOPE: reduce audit contention. The governance half is already done - authors now run SCOPED gates (touched modules + scalafmt + compileAll) and the full court is the chief's, once before a push. What remains for this bead: whether anything further is worth doing (build server, test parallelism settings, a lock or queue for full courts) or whether the governance change alone suffices - measure again after a period under the new rule before building anything. GUARDRAIL UNCHANGED AND NOW MORE IMPORTANT: do not cut ScalaCheck sample counts. That would have been the wrong fix to a misdiagnosed problem.
